title: A Reflection on Childbirth, Loss and Divine Comfort
text:
The writer recalls supporting a woman through labour while remembering the death of his mother from childbirth decades earlier. Drawing on faith, he reflects on the pain and resilience of women in labour, the presence of spiritual support and the belief that divine help is nearest in times of greatest need.
I sat on the middle edge of a birthing bed in one of the labour rooms of Duro Soleye Hospital, Ikeja, Lagos, on July 30, 1989.
My heart was pounding. My memory was connecting to August 5, 1959 when my mother bled to death in alabour room about three kilometers away. The baby in the womb of the woman beside me tended to be oblivious of my plea that he be born as quickly and as peacefully as possible.
He appeared to be enjoying himself in that safe, warm world in which responsibilities did not appear to exist, turning this way and that, sometimes kicking one side of the woman’s abdomen, making it bumpy this minute and flat the next. Sometimes, she shouted or cried in anguish as she became unable to bear the pain. In this situation, I could not emotionally reach her. If I could, I would remind her of our pet talks over meals.
They were to pave the way to this day. The summary was that every woman in labour was surrounded by Nature Beings who saw to the coming into being on earth of every soul borne by a woman. They are loving, dutiful, not intrusive and work helpfully. They are servants of the Almighty Creator who appoints willing women to this high task and does not abandon them when their need of Him is greatest.
Several years before now, my faith had taught me never in the face of tribulation to forget that “…WHEN THE NEED IS GREATEST, GOD’S HELP IS NEAREST TO YOU”! We only need to approach Him for it… “in calm confidence”. I have had cases of women who were delivered of their babies as if nothing happened. The woman beside me was resilient.
Her shouts were inaudible beyond the room. Even then I did not enjoy the sight I was beholding. I would pat her tremulous belly and run my fingers down her cheeks, reassuring her with the words… “I am with you”. Even then, I turned my face away each time she turned hers toward mine, lest she found me tearful, my eyes red.
I was emotionally connected with two women. I may look stoic and rough on the surface, but I remain very human within. The other woman on my mind was my mother. On that 30 July30, 1989 birthing, my memory went back and forth to August 5, 1959 when my mother died of excessive bleeding because she couldn’t expel the placenta.
This was at the then Ikeja General Hospital , about three kilometers away. The 30th anniversary of her passing was only five days away, and there I was, right beside a wife in prolonged labour. Orthodox hospitals are no-go areas for herbs except in the hands of a medical doctor who inherited them from herbalist fathers, or has learned about them. One of them is Dr. Ememobong, M.B.
, B.S. He transformed the practice of his herbalist father by infusing the wedding rings of his female patients with certain herbal extracts. This made them become contraceptive rings with one year guarantee. He had a thriving clinic at Ire Akari Estate near Okota, Lagos.
He saved many women from the side effects of contraceptive pills and intra-uterine devices , especially the copper variants. Another is a professor at the Lagos University Teaching Hospital . I learned of him from Mr Adeleke, a senior and experienced laboratory technologist of the pharmacognosy department of the College of Pharmacy of the University of Lagos located in the Teaching Hospital. Mr Adeleke was involved with research into Otunba Olajuwon Okubena’s JOBELYN, a master blood formula.
I approached him for help when I tried to stabilise OGBOLO , a parasitic root plant for promoting sperm production. As Editor of The GuardianU newspaper, I had directed a laboratory investigation by the newsroom’s Deklan Okpalaeke into the spermatogenesis potential of this root, and the report won the AFRICAN JOURNALIST OF THE YEAR AWARD for that year.
Mr Adeleke told me the LUTH obstetric and gynaecology professor had a native herbal soap inherited from his father which came in handy in his practice wherever he had a “difficult” patient. I sent to him women I knew could profit from this soap and they had good results. All he would do is massage the womb area with the soap lather. Even the most stubborn of babies would come down soon after.
Another person who did something close to that was Mrs Elizabeth Kafaru, now of blessed memory, but for incompetent cervix, another complication of pregnancy. The cervix, over which there is now so much noise about cervical cancer, is the “middle room” between the vagina , and the uterus. The cervix is made of fibrous connective tissues and soft muscles.
It has one “gateway” or “mouth” to the uterus above and another to the queen’s palace below. The opening to the uterus is expected to be firmly shut when there is a foetus in the uterus. If the cervix is “incompetent”, the opening of the uterus will give way after about three months of pregnancy and cause miscarriage. Many women suffer from miscarriages because of this.
In the hospital, a surgeon will stitch up the faulty opening to keep the baby in the uterus close to the time it is to be born. The stitches must be removed close to the birthing period for the baby to be born naturally and for the placenta to be expelled. Mrs Elizabeth Kafaru learned her procedure from top-notch but unsung herbalists. The method needed no surgery.
With an empty snail shell, she would scrape up the bark of a certain tree which her patient consumed to strengthen her cervix. Eating it tightened the opening of the cervix without the need for a surgical protocol. As with the surgeon’s intervention, Mrs Kafaru had to give her patient an antidote before the baby could be born naturally. The antidote was the reverse process of the remedy.
With an empty snail shell, she scraped DOWNWARDS the bark of the same tree and gave it to her patient in recipe form. The danger in this method was that the bark of that tree was not freely available on the health food store shelf. While another surgeon can remove the surgical stitches, not every herbalist would know of Mrs Kafaru’s protocol.
This, I believe was Otunba Okubena’s dilemma and objection to a recipe he received from some unsung traditional medicine fellows on how to check sexual frivolities among women especially spinsters. The remedy was a native hen’s egg into which the name of the patient’s mother’s maiden name was encoded under certain preparations before it was boiled and surreptitiously given to her to eat. The recipe guaranteed that no man who tried to access the Queen’s palace would have an erection.
The procedure could be reversed through another protocol. These are Nigerian traditional medicines orthodox doctors may wish to study and perfect for hospital use as well, and probably export them. Back to my wife and I in the labour room. Dr ADEKOLA, a surgeon so simple you could think he was a clerk in the office, could be friendly even with his surgical blade in his hand in the theatre, but he would not hear of uterine stimulants.
These are known to help the birthing process where uterine muscles are weak. I still wonder if they could not have helped my mother to expel the placenta, reduce the bleeding and, thereby, save her life. One of these herbs is RED RASPBERRY LEAVES. Another is Shepherd’s Purse.
Yet another is Yarrow. Beyond them can be a long list of an inexhaustible treasure trove of Mother Nature in this matter. Red Raspberry Leaves are well known for their toning effects on uterine and pelvic soft muscles. What helps them to do this is an active compound known as FRAGARINE.
Several studies say it makes the muscles contract more efficiently. This means a woman in the birthing process does not have to become energy deficient as many women are before they are delivered of their babies. Many herbalists give red raspberry leaves to their patients in the last trimester of pregnancy. They often complement it with a popular parasitic root which is known as OGBOLO in Yoruba land.
Many people know Ogbolo for its potential to help sperm production and to heal ulcers. Herbalists who know its value recommend it to pregnant women from a little after the middle of conception. In Benue State, women used ogbolo as a soup thickener. In Yoruba land, aging men consume the water extract as an anti-aging remedy.
In pregnant women, it is believed to make pelvic muscles more energetic and flexible. In many circles, red raspberry leaves are preferred for use before pregnancy. Often, it is used along with SHEPHERD’S PURSE, which is an astringent. This means it stops bleeding.
That is why it is useful in anemia caused by bleeding in any part of the body. In addition to this value in uterine bleeding, shepherd’s purse, with a shape similar to that of the uterus, helps to build the strength of uterine muscles. While we cannot underestimate yarrow, in any reproductive system ailments a woman may face, including bleeding in the labour room, another herb of choice in bleeding emergencies may be MIMOSA PUDICA.
It is also an astringent herb. Many people see it often, but regard it as a troublesome weed because it bears some spikes which stick to clothes in the fields. The Yorubas know of it and call it by a name appropriate for its astringent nature. That name is longish, though… PA ITAN RE MO, OKO RE N BO.
That means “close your lap, your husband is coming”. The plant testifies to this figurative expression. When the hand mistakenly or deliberately touches it, the two rows of leaves opposite each other on a vein in a stalk automatically close. The short form of its name for this behaviour is… PATANMO .
It is a way of saying it helps a woman whose paraphernalia are open and letting out too much blood. Always, I do not hesitate to ask women to use it if they bleed excessively during their periods. There are more herbs I would have liked to suggest for the labour room and other bleeding emergencies but for space.
While I was still beseeching the Lord for His help through Nature beings, and trying to imagine my mother in the labour room realising she may not return home to her family, I suddenly sighted Dr Adekola beside me, smiling. He congratulated me and my spirit lifted. I saw my wife asleep and ran my hand over her forehead and cheeks.
She opened her eyes, and I did the needful which I believed was all a humbled and loving man could do in a labour room for a wife who returned from what, to many women, was a chamber of death. Soon, the nurses brought to me the bundle of joy who had given us so much trouble.
I whispered his name into his ears, congratulated him for a successful journey to the earth and admonished him to judiciously expend his present sojourn on earth. A spiritual bandage over our physical vision and the intellect does not permit remembrance of events before we chose our parents in the light of our nature and, sometimes, serious or critical events which may have connected us in times gone by.
We may now have to sort out these events, seeds of which we sowed in previous eras. We must not assume that babies cannot read our intent or recognise us. I reported for The Guardian newspaper in the 1980s about an Argentine baby who spoke in the labour room, asking: “Where am I? Where is my family?
” As I handed my baby over to the midwife and took leave of my wife to do some things she requested I do, my mind swirled back to men and women, pregnancies, the labour room and child upbringing. Many men and women do not plan for pregnancy. They do not realise that the quality of sperm and the quality of egg will determine the quality of the baby they are going to have.
My wife and I were helped especially by two books… MALE SEXUAL VITALITY, by Michael T. Murray AND WOMEN’S BODY, WOMEN’S WISDOM, by Christiane Northrup, a gynaecologist of 35 years when she wrote it. The body must be detoxified of toxins, free radicals, heavy metals, etc. before pregnancy. The quality of sperm and egg is related to the quality of organs the coming baby would have. Eating fully and right are crucial.
Nature is kinder to the coming one. If the woman is deficient in calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, iron and vitamin E, for example, nature would pull from the little she has and give to the foetus which has none. That is why some women suffer bone loss, tooth decay and loss, weak muscles and even anemia during pregnancy. Omega-3 fatty acids are important and needed for brain formation, intelligence, healthy eyes and various organs.
Children whose mothers consumed lots of Omega-3 fats in their pregnancies have been shown to have more brain cells, be more intelligent and have healthier eyes often throughout life than children whose mothers did not. Every organ in the body needs this oil to protect it. When the house or wardrobe key does not turn well in the lock, what do we do? We drape it with palm oil or any other and, pronto, like magic, it behaves well!
Some women are hysterical after childbirth. The Yorubas call this condition… A BI SI WIN . In the language, this is post-natal psychosis or madness. What did the brain lose in pregnancy?
Many persons are unaware about the process of coming into being on earth. They imagine it is the sperm and egg which produce a human being. Yet, many of them have read the Bible and know of the ANNUNCIATION of the coming of the Lord Jesus and of the coming before Him of His Forerunner, John the Baptist.
The law which governed their coming governed the coming into being on earth of all of us, and will continue to govern the coming of more souls. The procreative act between a man and a woman is a petition for a soul out of many qualified ones in the “beyond” to be sent to them.
The woman in particular has the right and the duty to choose the type of soul she wants to inhabit the baby’s body growing in her womb by SERIOUSLY WILLING and avoiding circumstances which are not homogeneous with her desire. When she fails to establish this bridge or connection, a “black sheep” may find his or her way into the family.
This WILLING is crucial because it is in the middle of pregnancy that a soul hanging around the would-be mother enters into the growing baby’s body and takes possession of it. The woman’s demeanor dramatically changes when this happens as evidenced in the first kicks of pregnancy, and the establishment of the baby’s own blood circulation which, prior to this time, was carried out by the mother’s blood circulation.
It was to ensure that the mother of Jesus was able to attract only Him into the body growing within her womb that the Annunciation was made to her so that she could be INWARDLY CONNECTED WITH HIM. How many women today were inwardly connected with their children before they incarnated in the womb? Many parents today blame not themselves for the sexual misbehaviour of young persons. The misbehaviour is not necessarily what these children learned while growing up.
The seeds were sown in what they beheld when they were in the womb. Many doctors are guilty. They tell pregnant women sex throughout pregnancy tones pelvic muscles for the labour room. These doctors are too earthly in their understanding of LIFE.
They do not know that babies do see through the womb, despite enormous evidence that they respond to music. Another Biblical evidence which should have educated them was that when Mary, the mother of Jesus, went to visit her cousin, Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist, both babies in the womb were reported to have sighted each other across the womb barriers and “LEAPT WITH JOY”.
Baby Jesus came on a Mission, and Baby John the Baptist was to be His FORERUNNER in that Mission. How would they not leap with joy in the recognition that they had both set foot on earth and were awaiting their birth? Striving for purity ensures attraction of light souls for birth and exclusion of dark ones. Thus, we can say today’s sexually irresponsible children were attracted by sexually irresponsible mothers.
We can say, also, that many of today’s children reflect bad behaviour from the pre-natal bed.
